title: US Has Revoked More Than 175,000 Visas Under Trump, State Department Says
excerpt: The revocations — up 75% from the 100,000 milestone announced in January — target criminal activity, birth tourism, and political speech, as Indian student visa approvals drop 60%.
body:
• The U.S. State Department has revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump took office in January 2025, up from 100,000 announced seven months ago.
  • Leading causes include assault, DUI, theft, and drug crimes, with specific cases involving felony rape, kidnapping, and child sexual abuse material.
  • Indian student visa (F-1) approvals have dropped 60% compared to 2017, amid broader tightening of social media vetting and continuous screening.
  • The administration also revoked visas from birth tourism parents and foreigners who "celebrated" the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

The Trump administration has revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals, the U.S. State Department announced Monday, marking a sharp escalation in what has become the most aggressive immigration enforcement campaign in modern American history.

The figure, up 75% from the 100,000 milestone the department publicized in January, underscores the breadth of a crackdown that has extended well beyond undocumented immigrants to encompass visa holders accused of criminal activity, political speech deemed objectionable, and even maternity travel.

Criminal Activity Drives the Bulk of Revocations

Most visas were pulled following "law enforcement encounters," according to the department, with assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug offenses the leading causes. The department cited specific cases including a foreign national charged with felony rape and sexual battery, another facing kidnapping and human trafficking charges, and a person charged with more than a dozen counts of possessing child sexual abuse material.

https://x.com/StateDept/status/2087294958667472967

"A U.S. visa is a privilege, not a right. The Department remains committed to using every tool available to protect our communities from those who abuse it."

— U.S. State Department statement

A significant share of visas were also revoked for reckless driving, sexual assault, child abuse, fraud, and embezzlement, the department said. In one disclosed operation, a U.S. embassy in North Africa revoked more than 100 visas from parents allegedly engaged in birth tourism — traveling to the United States primarily so their children would receive U.S. citizenship.

Political Speech and the Charlie Kirk Cases

The department disclosed that it revoked visas from "multiple foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk," including one who said Kirk "died too late." The Kirk-related revocations have drawn particular scrutiny from civil liberties groups, who argue that revoking immigration privileges over political speech — even offensive speech — sets a dangerous precedent.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=LYEJi62DvpQ

Rights advocates and legal experts have broadly condemned the administration's expanded social media screening program, which they say functions as a surveillance apparatus that threatens free expression and disproportionately targets immigrants from certain regions.

Impact on Indian Nationals and Students

The crackdown has hit Indian nationals particularly hard. F-1 student visa approvals for Indian applicants fell 60% compared to the same period in 2017, according to Center for Immigration Studies data cited by the Washington Examiner. Chinese student visa approvals dropped 46% over the same period.

The decline comes alongside broader administrative tightening that includes enhanced social media vetting, expanded background screening, and a new Continuous Vetting Center designed to monitor all foreign nationals holding valid U.S. visas on an ongoing basis. State Department deputy spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the center ensures "all foreign nationals on American soil comply with our laws."

The Trajectory of Enforcement

The pace of revocations has accelerated steadily. The State Department reported approximately 80,000 revocations in November 2025, crossed 100,000 in January 2026, and has now reached 175,000 — a 150% increase from 2024 levels. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have also established operations at airports nationwide to screen for visa overstays.

At the same time, the administration dramatically reduced certain visa categories. The State Department suspended immigrant visa processing for nationals of 75 countries in January, citing "public charge" concerns, affecting family reunification and employment-based immigration.

What Comes Next

The administration has shown no signs of slowing down. Directives from the State Department have ordered U.S. diplomats abroad to scrutinize applicants with histories of political activism or those Washington views as potentially hostile. For Indians holding or seeking U.S. visas, the message is clear: the window of lenient enforcement that defined much of the past two decades has closed.
